b <- read.csv("results/sensitivity_diagnostics.csv")

row_for <- function(id, n, table = a) {
  row <- table[table$population_id == id & table$n == n, ]
  stopifnot(nrow(row) == 1L)
  row
}
for (i in seq_len(nrow(s))) {
  if (is.na(s$selected_n[i])) { stopifnot(s$population_id[i] == "cauchy"); next }
  row <- row_for(s$population_id[i], s$selected_n[i])
  columns <- c(skewness = "skewness_at_selected_n",
    excess_kurtosis = "excess_kurtosis_at_selected_n", qq_rmse = "qq_rmse_at_selected_n",

  for (name in names(columns)) stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(row[[name]], s[[columns[name]]][i])))
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(row_for(s$population_id[i], s$selected_n[i], b)$qq_rmse,
                            s$sensitivity_qq_rmse[i])))
}
options(knitr.kable.NA = "N/A")
format_metric <- function(x, digits = 3) ifelse(is.na(x), "N/A", sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f"), x))
table_print <- function(x, digits = 3, widths = rep("1fr", ncol(x))) {
  stopifnot(length(widths) == ncol(x))
  values <- as.data.frame(lapply(x, function(column) {
    if (is.numeric(column)) format_metric(column, digits) else
      ifelse(is.na(column), "N/A", as.character(column))
  }))
  cells <- c(names(x), as.vector(t(as.matrix(values))))
  cat("```{=typst}\n#table(columns: (", paste(widths, collapse = ", "),
      "), align: left,\n", paste0("text(", encodeString(cells, quote = '\"'), ")", collapse = ",\n"),
      "\n)\n```\n\n", sep = "")
}

**The answer is population-specific.** I investigated how large one sample must be for its average to have a useful Normal approximation. The practical choices range from exact Normality at n = 1 to a qualified dependent-process choice at 350. Cauchy has no finite answer.

# 02 / Three questions, three answers

**Research question:** What is the smallest tested n at which I am comfortable calling the sampling distribution of the sample mean approximately Normal?

## Question 1 / How large must n be?

**There is no universal n=30.** Thirty exceeds the Normal, die and age choices, but clearer departures remain for Exponential, small Binomial, basketball and dependent failure. It cannot repair Cauchy.

**Fastest:** Normal is exact at 1. The symmetric bounded die (10) and bounded synthetic mixture (15) are fast non-Normal iid cases. An irregular population is not necessarily slow.

**Slower:** Exponential (90) retains right skew; Binomial (75) and basketball (140) retain discrete gaps. Basketball has small skew at its choice, yet steps matter. Dependent failure (350) is the slowest finite empirical choice, with extra uncertainty about asymptotic behavior.

```{=typst}
#context [*I base this conclusion on* the master results (page #counter(page).at(<results>).first()), the eight evidence cards (pages #counter(page).at(<cards>).first()-#counter(page).at(<stress-tests>).first()), and smaller-n comparisons (page #counter(page).at(<boundary>).first()).]
#parbreak()
```

## Question 2 / What counts as approximately Normal?

A bell-shaped histogram alone was not enough. Q-Q curvature/steps, skewness, excess kurtosis and nearby stability supported my practical choices, not a single p-value. No numerical pass/fail cutoff was used. These choices do not certify extreme-tail accuracy.

```{=typst}
#context [*I base this conclusion on* the explicit decision standard and Normal calibration (page #counter(page).at(<method>).first()), plus the graphical and numerical boundary evidence (pages #counter(page).at(<cards>).first()-#counter(page).at(<boundary>).first()).]
#parbreak()
```

## Question 3 / What if CLT assumptions fail?

Cauchy's tails invalidate the ordinary finite-variance theorem. Dependence retains covariance terms in Var(Xbar). Independent non-identical shots can still have a useful approximation with their individual variances. Symmetry, skew, discreteness, boundedness and dependence mattered here; no one property explained every result.

```{=typst}
#context [*I base this conclusion on* the extra-credit and Cauchy cards (pages #counter(page).at(<extra-mixture-shots>).first()-#counter(page).at(<stress-tests>).first()), the special-case interpretation (page #counter(page).at(<complicated>).first()), and appropriate mean/SE checks (page #counter(page).at(<moments>).first()).]
#parbreak()
```

**Limit:** the ranking depends on this tolerance and tested grid. Stricter tail accuracy could require larger n. More B improves simulation precision; it does not repair a violated assumption. Borderline neighboring choices may also be defensible.

# 03 / AI helped; iteration improved the argument

The initial prompt asked AI for a professional reusable R/Quarto project with eight cases, B = 10,000, calibration and no invented conclusions. I requested clear decisions and evidence-backed reasons rather than complicated output.

```{r}
table_print(data.frame(Stage = c("Build","Technical audit","Boundary reasoning","Final report"),
  `AI contribution / check` = c("Generators, simulation, diagnostics, Quarto","Found overwrite/shared-grid defects; fixed and tested them","Smaller candidates, plots and two-seed comparisons","Compressed 35 pages; checked results and layout"),
  `My actual input` = c("Specified scope, R, reproducibility and understandable code","Requested careful correction; did not personally find the code bugs","Questioned prettier plots; approved practical tolerance","Required a concise submission with clear answers and evidence"),check.names = FALSE),
  widths = c("0.8fr", "1.8fr", "1.8fr"))
```

### A real exchange, not an invented iteration

**My follow-up:** "They looked better. But I didn't know ... we need the smallest defensible n. Maybe then going off visually isn't right?"

**Weakness:** nicer larger-n plots did not explain why smaller values were unacceptable. Demanding exact-Normal simulation noise was too strict for a practical approximation.

**Revision:** targeted smaller-n checks, below/at/above comparisons, fixed alternate seed and explicit borderline reservations. Die 9 versus 10 now acknowledges ambiguity rather than a manufactured sharp boundary.

**Validation:** both seeds' saved vectors reproduce their rows; seeded replay preserves the machine recurrence; tests verify varying basketball probabilities, their SE and age moments. These are computational/theoretical checks, not a claim that AI is an independent reviewer.

### Understanding the important methods

One generator call creates n observations; one mean produces one number; B repetitions create the sampling distribution. Histograms show central shape, Q-Q bends show distributional mismatch, and correct mean/SE does not establish shape. Cauchy's population moments are undefined even when a finite sample average is calculable. These distinctions were clarified during the recorded review; complete line-by-line mastery is not claimed.

**Decision ownership:** AI proposed the working integers under the practical standard I approved. My contribution was specifying the task, questioning the smallest-n argument and requesting corrections and validation. The log separates those roles; it does not invent personal predictions, reactions or independent code audits.

The AI log records four selected real exchanges and validation, not a complete transcript. Reconstructed response summaries are labeled; important-code explanations remain in the separate investigations.

# 04 / What counts as normal enough?

My standard is a **useful central-shape approximation**, not exact Normality or certified accuracy for rare tail probabilities. Small residual bends and discrete steps may be acceptable. No single diagnostic, hypothesis test or p-value decides the result. The project used **no numerical pass/fail cutoffs**.

```{r}
table_print(data.frame(
  Evidence = c("Histogram", "Normal Q-Q plot", "Skewness / excess kurtosis", "Q-Q RMSE", "Mean / SE", "Stability"),
  `What I looked for` = c("A broadly symmetric, unimodal bell", "No substantial systematic curvature", "Modest asymmetry and tail discrepancy", "Smaller standardized rank discrepancies", "Agreement with valid theoretical references", "Similar conclusions nearby and under seed 7617"),
  `Role in the decision` = c("Visual support, not enough alone", "Separate tail bends from lattice steps", "Describe departures; no rigid thresholds", "Compare candidates and Normal noise", "Check implementation; spread is not shape", "Avoid one unusually nice plot"),
  check.names = FALSE), widths = c("1fr", "1.4fr", "1.4fr"))
```

### Monte Carlo design

At each n I generate **B = 10,000 fresh samples**, average the n observations in each, then diagnose the B means. This is not bootstrapping an observed dataset. The original population does not become Normal; its averages may.

The 15-value coarse grid spans n=1-500. Population-specific refinements and large-n checks produced **`r nrow(a)` tested case/n combinations per seed**. Smaller candidates and nearby larger values informed the choices; the detailed files retain the progression.

Seed **7616** starts the fixed-order primary experiment; **7617** starts the identical alternate design. Targeted boundary experiments reset their assigned seed before each experiment. Seed and experiment order both matter.

### Calibration: a reference, not a cutoff

Thirty genuinely Normal experiments at each coarse n (each B = 10,000) quantify simulation noise. At n = 1 their empirical 2.5th-97.5th percentile ranges were:

```{r}
c1 <- cal[cal$n == 1, ]
table_print(data.frame(Diagnostic = c("Skewness", "Excess kurtosis", "Q-Q RMSE"),
  `Normal-only noise range` = c(
    sprintf("%.3f to %.3f", c1$skewness_q025, c1$skewness_q975),
    sprintf("%.3f to %.3f", c1$excess_kurtosis_q025, c1$excess_kurtosis_q975),
    sprintf("%.3f to %.3f", c1$qq_rmse_q025, c1$qq_rmse_q975)), check.names = FALSE))
```

These are empirical ranges, not exact tolerance limits; accepted cases can remain outside this noise under the practical standard.

**Reading the plots:** histograms show sample means; orange Normal overlays use valid theoretical mean/SE only. Q-Q lines are fitted quartile references. Discrete bins respect the 1/n lattice. QQ RMSE compares sorted, empirically standardized means with standard-Normal rank quantiles; it is descriptive, not proof.

**Expectations:** no pre-run personal predictions were recorded. The card expectations are retrospective theory.

# 10 / Why not a smaller n?

Actual tested neighbors are compared below, not hypothetical failures between them. QQ is primary-seed Q-Q RMSE. Full graphical progression stays in the separate investigations.

```{r}
finite <- s[!is.na(s$selected_n), ]
qq_cell <- function(id, n) {
  if (is.na(n)) return("None below 1")
  paste0(n, ": ", format_metric(row_for(id, n)$qq_rmse))
}
table_print(data.frame(Case = labels[finite$population_id],
  `Lower n: QQ` = mapply(qq_cell, finite$population_id, finite$below_n),
  `Choice n: QQ` = mapply(qq_cell, finite$population_id, finite$selected_n),
  `Higher n: QQ` = mapply(qq_cell, finite$population_id, finite$above_n),
  Reservation = c("Exact at 1", "9 is borderline", "80 varies across seeds", "60 has coarser steps", "300 has more skew", "125 has clearer gaps", "12 bends more left"), check.names = FALSE),
  widths = c("1.3fr", "1fr", "1fr", "1fr", "1.5fr"))
```

### Improvement is not a sudden switch

Die 9 and 10 are close, as are age 12 and 15. I do not claim every smaller integer fails: some were not tested and neighboring choices may be defensible under a looser tolerance. The selected value is a first convincing practical compromise within this grid.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.6
#| fig-cap: "Exponential local search: both fixed seeds fluctuate around broadly improving shape. The highlighted 90 is a judgment, not a numerical-threshold crossing."
ns <- c(60,75,80,90,100,110,150)
x <- a[a$population_id == "exponential" & a$n %in% ns, ]
y <- b[b$population_id == "exponential" & b$n %in% ns, ]
par(mar = c(3.5,4,1,1), mgp = c(2,.5,0))
plot(x$n,x$qq_rmse,type = "b",pch = 16,col = "#007D83",lwd = 2,
     ylim = range(c(x$qq_rmse,y$qq_rmse)),xlab = "Sample size n",ylab = "Q-Q RMSE")
lines(y$n,y$qq_rmse,type = "b",pch = 1,col = "#D66B32",lwd = 2)
points(90,row_for("exponential",90)$qq_rmse,pch = 21,cex = 1.8,bg = "white",col = "#007D83")
legend("topright",c("Seed 7616","Seed 7617"),col = c("#007D83","#D66B32"),pch = c(16,1),lty = 1,bty = "n",cex = .9)
```

**Why it matters:** a larger n can have a worse finite-B diagnostic than its neighbor. The prettiest plot or first low QQ score would overstate boundary precision. Concordant visual evidence, valid theory and stability support the choice; uncertainty remains.

# 11 / Where the CLT became complicated

```{r}
table_print(data.frame(Case = c("Cauchy","Dependent failure","Basketball shots","Synthetic age mixture"),
  `What happened` = c("Extreme Q-Q departures remain at 5000","Empirical means form a bell near 350","Fine steps remain near 140 despite small skew","Irregular population smooths by 15"),
  `Why / conclusion` = c("Averages stay Cauchy; missing moments make this impossible, not slow","Covariance changes variance; empirical approximation, no proved dependent CLT","Independence survives, identical distribution does not; sum individual variances","Bounded iid observations; complexity alone does not imply slow convergence"),check.names = FALSE),
  widths = c("0.85fr", "1.6fr", "2fr"))
```

### Heavy tails: apparent stability can mislead

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.15
#| fig-cap: "One Cauchy path, seed 7616. Jumps persist through 5,000 observations. Zero marks location, not population mean; one path is not a sampling distribution."
set.seed(student_seed)
par(mar = c(3.5,4,1,1),mgp = c(2,.5,0))
x <- cauchy_generator(5000)
plot(seq_along(x),cumsum(x)/seq_along(x),type = "l",col = "#007D83",lwd = 1.5,
     xlab = "Observations accumulated",ylab = "Running mean")
abline(h = 0,col = "#D66B32",lty = 2)
```

Cauchy's characteristic function is exp(-abs(t)); independence gives exp(-abs(t)/n)^n = exp(-abs(t)) for its average. It keeps the same law at every n. Simulation illustrates this theory; a finite search alone would not prove impossibility.

### Dependence and mixtures: different complications

Long operating times raise the next failure rate, creating a compensating pattern. Individual second moments are bounded because rates are at least exp(-1.25), but a dependent CLT is not established. Covariance and the initial condition prevent borrowing the iid SE.

The synthetic age model stays iid and bounded: weights .045 exp(-age/5) + .030 exp(-.5((age-65)/10)²), normalized on 0-100. Fast smoothing contrasts with the right-skewed Exponential; it is **not** a historical mortality claim or a result about every mixture.

# 12 / Validation: moments and a second seed

SE is the SD of the B simulated means, not individual observations. Agreement with theory checks center/spread; it does not establish a Normal shape.

```{r}
#| results: asis
cat("```{=typst}\n#set text(size: 9.5pt)\n```\n\n")
table_print(data.frame(Case = labels[s$population_id],
  n = ifelse(is.na(s$selected_n),"None",s$selected_n),
  `Mean sim.` = s$empirical_mean_at_selected_n, `Mean theory` = s$theoretical_mean,
  `SE sim.` = s$empirical_se_at_selected_n, `SE theory` = s$theoretical_se_or_reference,
  `SE error %` = 100*s$relative_se_error,check.names = FALSE),digits = 4,
  widths = c("1.6fr", "0.5fr", "1fr", "1fr", "1fr", "1fr", "1fr"))
cat("\n\n```{=typst}\n#set text(size: 10.5pt)\n```\n\n")
```

**Appropriate references:** iid finite-variance cases use SE = sigma/sqrt(n). Basketball uses mean(p_i) and Var(Xbar) = sum[p_i(1-p_i)]/n²; its mean is .70 for n>=2, .90 for n=1.

```{r}
#| include: false
p <- nonidentical_probabilities(s$selected_n[s$population_id == "nonidentical_bernoulli"])
```

At basketball n=140, correct SE is `r format_metric(sqrt(sum(p*(1-p))/length(p)^2),5)`, versus `r format_metric(sqrt(mean(p)*(1-mean(p))/length(p)),5)` from the incorrect identical-p shortcut. Cauchy has no population moment targets. The dependent process has no supplied analytic mean/SE; baseline mean 1 is not the full-process target.

### Exponential boundary: seeds 7616 and 7617

The alternate run repeats all `r nrow(a)` case/n combinations at B = 10,000. These are actual boundary rows, not a search for favorable seeds.

```{r}
seed_rows <- do.call(rbind,lapply(c(80,90,100),function(n) {
  z <- rbind(row_for("exponential",n),row_for("exponential",n,b))
  data.frame(n = as.character(n),Seed = c("7616","7617"),Mean = z$empirical_mean,SE = z$empirical_se,
             Skew = z$skewness,Kurt. = z$excess_kurtosis,QQ = z$qq_rmse)
}))
table_print(seed_rows,digits = 4,widths = c("0.65fr", "0.8fr", rep("1fr", 5)))
```

**Seed conclusion:** exact diagnostics change, but n=90 remains a defensible central approximation under both seeds. The greater discrepancy at 80 supports its borderline reservation. The same working choices remain practical candidates; an automatic algorithm did not independently rediscover every integer.

**Reproducibility:** seed directories are separate, and saved vectors reproduce CSV B, mean, SD and QQ. The October 6 fresh-directory full rerun matched generated tables byte-for-byte on the same R version. This revision rechecks saved evidence, not a new full simulation. Detailed investigations retain the all-population seed comparisons.

# 13 / Conclusions and the evidence archive

1. **No universal n=30:** practical choices span 1-350; Cauchy has no finite choice.
2. **Shape matters, complexity alone does not:** the bounded age mixture smooths faster than the right-skewed Exponential.
3. **Discreteness is not automatic failure:** useful die, Binomial and basketball approximations can retain Q-Q steps.
4. **Moment agreement is not shape agreement:** mean/SE checks must accompany graphical and shape evidence.
5. **Assumptions change the answer:** Cauchy lacks moments, machine times require covariance, and shots require individual probabilities.
6. **A boundary needs an argument:** nearby evidence, theory and two seeds matter more than one pretty plot or isolated score. Borderline minima remain uncertain.

## Detailed analysis-file map

Paths are relative to [github.com/babaJaan01/Monte_Carlo_CLT](https://github.com/babaJaan01/Monte_Carlo_CLT). Each `.qmd` contains population/theory, tested progression, plots, justification, limitations and seed comparison. Rendered HTML has matching basenames in `docs/analyses/`.

```{r}
analysis_files <- c("01_standard_normal","02_six_sided_die","03_exponential","04_binomial_small",
                    "05_cauchy","06_extra_dependent_failure","07_extra_nonidentical_bernoulli","08_extra_age_at_death")
paths <- paste0("analyses/",analysis_files,".qmd")
stopifnot(all(file.exists(paths)))
table_print(data.frame(Population = unname(labels),`Detailed analysis file` = paths,check.names = FALSE),
  widths = c("1fr", "3fr"))
```

**Results / plots:** primary, sensitivity and final-summary CSVs in `results/`; judgments in `decisions.csv`; summary visuals in `figures/`; individual plots in `docs/analyses/`. Mean vectors are regenerated, not tracked in Git.

**Reproduce:** restore `renv.lock`, run `scripts/run_project.R`, `scripts/validate_results.R`, `scripts/render_summary.R`, then `quarto render`. Statistics use base R; knitr/rmarkdown support rendering; Quarto supplies Typst. Exact commands are in README.

**Sources:** original guidance, Class 05 CLT and Class 06 distributions/project lessons, plus all three instructor models, remain unchanged in `references/`. Updated guidance defines five required and three extra cases. Expectations are retrospective; no undocumented personal prediction or surprise is manufactured.
